content_voiceover: This slide covers the Khorana score, a validated predictive model for chemotherapy associated venous thromboembolism, which is heavily tested on hematology boards. The score assigns points based on several patient characteristics. Site of cancer matters most, very high risk sites like stomach and pancreas get two points, while high risk sites like lung, lymphoma, gynecologic, bladder, and testicular cancers get one point. Additional points are given for a prechemotherapy platelet count of three hundred fifty times ten to the ninth per liter or more, a hemoglobin below one hundred grams per liter or use of red cell growth factors, a prechemotherapy leukocyte count above eleven times ten to the ninth per liter, and a body mass index of thirty five or higher. Each of these adds one point. The bar graph below shows how well this score stratifies risk, patients scoring zero, the low risk group, have a VTE rate under one percent, intermediate risk patients with a score of one to two have around two percent, and high risk patients with a score of three or more have a VTE rate of roughly seven percent, similar in both the development and validation cohorts. Clinically, a Khorana score of two or higher is often used to identify outpatients who may benefit from thromboprophylaxis during chemotherapy.
keypoints: Khorana score predicts chemotherapy-associated VTE risk
Stomach and pancreas cancer score highest, two points
One point each for high-risk cancer site, high platelets, low hemoglobin, high leukocytes, high BMI
Low score under one percent VTE risk, high score around seven percent
Score of two or more often used to guide outpatient thromboprophylaxis decisions
keypoint_voiceover: The Khorana score combines cancer site, platelet count, hemoglobin, leukocyte count, and BMI to stratify chemotherapy patients into low, intermediate, and high VTE risk, with high risk patients approaching a seven percent event rate.
